11/20/2026
Share

Since the beginning of November, the cost of transporting crude oil via Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) has fallen sharply. This decline reflects both weakening demand for VLCC charters and the fading of the geopolitical risk premium that had previously driven freight rates to historic highs in October.
Data from the Baltic Exchange shows that on November 13, VLCC freight rates on the Gulf of Oman to China route (as measured by the Worldscale index) fell to approximately 308 points, a sharp drop of 64% from the all-time high (841 points) reached on October 8.
As VLCC freight rates plummet, oil-exporting nations in the Gulf have ramped up their crude exports to levels seen before the onset of the U.S.-Iran conflict. Despite ongoing attacks on vessels, the market has managed to sustain crude outflows through workarounds such as ship-to-ship transfers and “dark voyages”—where tankers disable their tracking signals to evade detection. This rise in crude exports from the Gulf has dampened demand for oil from other regions, thereby freeing up VLCC capacity.

Delia He, an analyst at Arrow Shipbroking, noted: “Crude exports from the Gulf have recently rebounded to near pre-conflict levels, which has reduced demand among Asian buyers for crude from the U.S. and the North Sea—and, consequently, lowered the demand for tanker charters.”
Vortexa analyst Ioannis Papadimitriou stated: “The recent surge in freight rates has dampened demand in the Asian market for long-haul crude oil—such as that from the U.S., West Africa, and the North Sea—prompting Asia to increase its procurement of crude from the Middle East instead. This shift has led to a decline in demand for Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) on long-haul routes. Meanwhile, the available capacity in the market has continued to rise as vessels complete their discharge operations in East Asia. This influx of additional capacity is exerting downward pressure on freight rates.”
Beyond the route from the Gulf of Oman to China, freight rates on other routes—such as those from West Africa to Asia—have experienced even sharper declines.
The surge in VLCC freight rates was partly driven by market concerns over heightened operational risks in the Persian Gulf—such as the mutual targeting of oil tankers by the U.S. and Iran—a factor that also pushed up oil prices. This month, crude oil futures (LCOc1) have fallen by 20%, partly due to the potential for an easing of tensions with Iran.
Delia He noted: “The significant pullback in VLCC freight rates is only partially rooted in market fundamentals; such extreme volatility essentially reflects an over-correction of the geopolitical risk premium.”

Hormuz Tanker Attacks Collide with Sliding Crude Prices

CMB News Editorial
Editorial Desk
November 20, 2026
       
Intensified tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz raise supply and freight risks just as Brent crude prices slide on oversupply fears. Concise crude oil market view.
Renewed attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz are sharply increasing route and freight risk just as crude benchmarks slide on oversupply concerns, creating a rare mix of geopolitical tension and softening prices. For now, physical flows from the Persian Gulf remain substantial but more volatile, keeping a latent risk premium in an otherwise weakening market. Crude traders face a conflicted backdrop: higher-frequency and more severe attacks on Hormuz oil and LPG tankers, with incidents now occurring almost daily in October and November, coincide with Middle East exports approaching pre-war levels and the IEA signalling that global supply is again outpacing demand. Brent futures have retreated roughly 15–20% over the past month, recently oscillating around the low 90s USD/bbl range, even as maritime security agencies report a steady drumbeat of strikes and mining events near Iran and Oman.

Supply & Demand

The key development is the sharp escalation in attacks on oil and LPG tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz since October, attributed to Iranian forces and allied groups. Maritime incident data from UKMTO and commercial trackers indicate roughly one reported attack per day in Hormuz so far in November, including vessels struck by projectiles, limpet mines and suspected sea mines, alongside at least one large tanker fire and missing seafarers.

...

Fundamentals & Freight

The attacks are increasingly targeting larger crude and product carriers, including supertankers, and in some cases the same vessel is reportedly struck multiple times to hinder salvage efforts. This raises not only direct cargo risk but also effective fleet capacity loss, as damaged tonnage is withdrawn and owners reroute ships away from the highest‑risk lanes.

...

Short-Term Outlook & Trading View

In the very near term (next 1–2 weeks), the market will likely remain caught between bearish fundamentals and bullish risk headlines. Unless a major, multi‑day halt of Hormuz traffic occurs, the current structural picture still points to modest oversupply, with further downside risk for flat prices if macro data weaken or if non‑OPEC producers maintain high output. Conversely, any high‑profile incident—such as the total loss of a fully laden VLCC or confirmed mining of the main traffic separation scheme—could rapidly reprice a "war premium" across the curve. Trading outlook (directional, not investment advice)
* Short‑term bias: cautiously bearish on flat Brent while it trades in the high‑80s to low‑90s USD/bbl range, given evidence of supply exceeding demand and compressed spreads.
* Upside risk: significant tail risk of sharp, headline‑driven spikes on news of severe tanker damage or temporary closure of parts of Hormuz; consider hedging short exposure or using optional structures rather than outright unhedged shorts.
* Spreads & cracks: watch prompt Brent spreads and Middle East sour–sweet differentials; tightening spreads or widening freight could signal that attacks are materially tightening physical availability despite weak macro demand.

China has officially extended the suspension of export controls on certain rare earth elements that was due to end on Nov. 10 to Jan. 10 next year.
The suspension covering export controls on five rare earth elements — holmium, erbium, thulium, europium and ytterbium — as well as certain technologies and equipment used in rare earth processing, was announced by China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) on Nov. 9.
Additional export restrictions on certain lithium batteries, graphite materials and products manufactured overseas using Chinese-origin rare earths will also remain suspended.
Meanwhile, export controls introduced in April 2025 on seven other rare earth elements — samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium and yttrium — remain in effect.
MOFCOM's announcement follows the extension of trade arrangements between China and the US, announced after a Sept. 28 summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House.
The announcement highlights China's influence across rare earth and critical mineral supply chains. China's export controls on rare earths and battery materials

Some of China's controls on rare earths, critical metals and battery technology are in force today. A larger package from October 2025 is suspended, now until January 10, 2027 under an announcement of November 9, 2026. This page separates the two, with each measure's announcement number so you can check it.

How to read Chinese export-control notices

China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) issues each measure as a numbered announcement, often jointly with the General Administration of Customs. Among the measures below, only Announcement No. 18 of 2025 has an official English text on MOFCOM's English site, and MOFCOM marks even that one "for reference only"; the Chinese text is authentic. The other descriptions on this page are our English summaries of Chinese-only texts, with links to the originals.
Since December 1, 2024, the controlled items sit in one Dual-Use Items Export Control List ( Announcement No. 51 of 2024 ), licensed under State Council Decree No. 792. The same announcement repealed the separate 2023–2024 notices on gallium, germanium, graphite and antimony and moved their items into the list. Articles that still cite those older notice numbers as live are out of date; the items remain controlled under the list.

In force today

* Measure | What it controls | Since
* No. 18 of 2025 (English text available) | Seven medium and heavy rare earths: samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium, yttrium. Includes samarium-cobalt magnet material and NdFeB magnet material containing terbium or dysprosium. | April 4, 2025
* No. 10 of 2025 | Tungsten, tellurium, bismuth, molybdenum and indium items | February 4, 2025
* Dual-use list (No. 51 of 2024) | Gallium, germanium, antimony, graphite (including natural flake and spherical graphite) and superhard-material items: a license is needed for every destination | Controlled since 2023–2024

The April 2025 rare-earth controls were never suspended. A magnet buyer whose material contains terbium or dysprosium has needed its Chinese supplier to hold a license since April 2025, whatever happens to the suspensions.

On November 9, 2026, MOFCOM and the General Administration of Customs published No. 58 of 2026 (in Chinese): "from November 11, 2026 to January 10, 2027", Announcements No. 55, 56, 57, 58, 61 and 62 of 2025 remain suspended. No. 70 of 2025 had suspended them until November 10, so there is no gap. Do not confuse No. 58 of 2026, the suspension, with No. 58 of 2025, the battery-materials control it suspends.
This puts into law what MOFCOM announced on September 28, 2026, when it wrote that both sides had agreed to extend the Kuala Lumpur arrangement to January 10, 2027 ( MOFCOM, in Chinese ). The new date is two months away, not a year.
The November 27 date for the US-specific clause is a separate suspension (No. 72 of 2025), and as of November 10, 2026 nothing we found moves it. Watch MOFCOM's announcement list before November 27.

Notices are usually cited by number and year. This is each one that matters for these materials, what it does and where it stands on November 10, 2026. * The Chinese exporter applies, to MOFCOM. The buyer cannot apply for it (Announcement No. 18; Decree No. 792).

Yttrium oxide costs x125 more in Europe than China as export restrictions split the rare earths market

* November 11, 2026
* By Christian Purefoy
* yttrium oxide costs about US$1.15 million a tonne in Europe against US$9,144 in China , roughly x125 more, according to Argus Media prices reported by Bloomberg, while Benchmark put North American yttrium oxide at about x196 the Chinese price at the end of September
* Shanghai Metals Market quoted European dysprosium oxide at US$3,300-4,200/kg on November 5, against US$215-220/kg in China, about x15 to x19, and Platts assessed dysprosium oxide in North America at US$4,100/kg on October 30, with terbium oxide at US$8,100/kg
* China exported 934 tonnes of yttrium oxide in January-September 2026 , 26% less than a year earlier, with only 18 tonnes going to Japan, down 98%, according to customs data reported by Kyodo and Mysteel , and China’s pause on a wider set of export controls leaves its April 2025 curbs on seven heavy rare earths, including yttrium, dysprosium and terbium, in force
Yttrium oxide now costs at least x125 more in Europe than in China, as Beijing’s export restrictions on heavy rare earths split the market in two.
A metric tonne of the oxide costs about US$1.15 million in Europe, compared with US$9,144 in China , according to Argus Media prices reported by Bloomberg . Supplies inside China remain substantial and, before the curbs, prices around the world were only slightly higher than in China.
The gap comes after China extended its pause on a wider set of rare earth export controls until January 10 , 2027 — but that extension does not touch the metals behind the price gap. Controls introduced in April 2025 on samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium and yttrium remain in effect , and exporters still need a licence.

How wide is the gap?

The price difference may be even higher, with Benchmark putting North American yttrium oxide at about x196 the Chinese price at the end of September 2026.
Dysprosium, which keeps magnets working at high temperatures, shows a similar split: on November 5, Shanghai Metals Market quoted European dysprosium oxide at US$3,300-4,200/kg , against US$215-220/kg in China, about x15 to x19. Benchmark had already put European dysprosium oxide at around x16.3 the Chinese price at the end of September, up from x6.8 at the end of June.
The chart below shows those multiples, by source and date:
Horizontal bar chart of prices outside China as a multiple of the Chinese price: yttrium oxide CIF North America x196 (Benchmark, end-September 2026); yttrium oxide Europe x125 (Argus Media via Bloomberg, 10 November 2026); dysprosium oxide Europe x17.2 (SMM midpoint, 5 November 2026) and x16.3 (Benchmark, end-September 2026).
In North America, the story is the same, with Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessing dysprosium oxide in North America at US$4,100/kg on October 30 , up from US$1,200/kg when the assessment was launched on March 31. Terbium oxide rose from US$4,900/kg to US$8,100/kg over the same period, and samarium oxide from US$175/kg to US$1,200/kg.
The chart below shows those Platts assessments on March 31 and October 30:
Paired bar chart of Platts CIF North America rare earth oxide prices in US dollars per kilogram: dysprosium oxide US$1,200 on 31 March 2026 and US$4,100 on 30 October 2026; terbium oxide US$4,900 and US$8,100; samarium oxide US$175 and US$1,200.
The prices reflect a real shortage of material, not just speculation.
China exported 934 tonnes of yttrium oxide in January-September 2026 , 26% less than a year earlier, according to customs data reported by Kyodo. Only 18 tonnes went to Japan , down 98% from 887 tonnes in the same period of 2025. Mysteel, citing the General Administration of Customs, recorded 110.061 tonnes in September alone.

Why yttrium matters

Yttrium is used in semiconductors and coats the blades of gas and jet-engine turbines, so the squeeze reaches across defence, aerospace and the power supply for artificial intelligence data centres.
Most mined yttrium still comes from China , despite efforts by the US to support a secure, ex-China supply. For example, Lynas Rare Earths is expanding heavy rare earth production at its Malaysian plant, but yttrium is sequenced after gadolinium and is not yet in production.
Project Blue research director David Merriman warned that little relief is coming soon :
“Within the next year or two, really there is very limited ex-China supply which is going to be available”
The Pentagon’s ban on Chinese rare earths in defence supply chains starts on January 1 , and the US has already warned Beijing that it has delivered only two-thirds of its commitments . Japan has already seen the squeeze, as we reported .

The price signal cuts both ways

The squeeze is in heavy rare earths, not the whole market.
Outside China, prices for praseodymium-neodymium oxide, the main light rare earth used in magnets, fell below the US$110/kg floor set in MP Materials’ and Lynas’s agreements with the US Department of Defense during the third quarter, as producers outside China redirected volumes into an oversupplied market.

US demand drives sharp increases in CIP global terbium, dysprosium prices

Prices for the magnetic heavy rare earths dysprosium and terbium outside China rose sharply in the week ended Thursday October 1, with market participants pointing to strong US demand ahead of new defense-sector sourcing restrictions due to take effect in January 2027.

October 6, 2026
By Sebastian Evelyn and Henry Sanderson
Aerospace and Defense China Rare earths United States
Key takeaways:
* US defense sourcing rules are tightening: Anticipation of January 2027 Pentagon restrictions on China-linked rare earth magnets is driving increased demand and higher prices for dysprosium and terbium outside China.
* Heavy rare earth prices have surged: Dysprosium, terbium and ferro-dysprosium recorded sharp weekly gains as buyers compete for limited non-Chinese supply.
* Technology is reducing intensity, not eliminating demand: Magnet producers continue to lower dysprosium and terbium usage per unit through innovation, but both elements remain critical for high-performance applications.

US defense restrictions drive buying interest

The increase in demand comes ahead of US Department of Defense sourcing restrictions that will prohibit the Pentagon from procuring samarium-cobalt and neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) magnets containing materials mined, refined, separated, melted or produced in China from January 2027.
Market participants said US consumers were willing to pay significantly higher prices for material than buyers in Europe, raising prices across global markets.

Heavy rare earth prices jump

Fastmarkets’ price assessment for terbium oxide 99.99%, cip global rose by 41% to $5,000-8,000 per kg on Thursday, from $4,200-5,000 per kg on September 24.
US demand boosts ex-China terbium prices
Fastmarkets’ price assessment for dysprosium oxide 99.5%, cip global rose to $2,500-3,500 per kg on Thursday from $1,910-2,500 per kg a week earlier.
Fastmarkets’ ferro-dysprosium 80%, cip global assessment increased to $2,750-3,850 per kg on the same day from $1,375-2,100 per kg a week earlier, marking one of the strongest weekly gains across the rare earths market.
US buyers push dysprosium oxide prices higher
Dysprosium and terbium are typically added in small quantities to NdFeB permanent magnets to improve magnetic performance and heat resistance, making them essential inputs for high-performance applications including electric vehicles, wind turbines and defence systems.
Ferro-dysprosium is also used in certain magnet alloys and specialist applications.

Alternative supply chains gain momentum

Several companies and governments outside China have stepped up efforts to develop alternative supplies of dysprosium and terbium, reflecting growing concern over the concentration of heavy rare earth production and processing in China.
Australian miner Lynas announced on September 30 it will acquire Meteoric Resources for A$968 million ($633.5 million), giving it access to the company’s dysprosium- and terbium-containing Caldeira project. The company said the project could eventually produce 127 tonnes per year of the two heavy rare earths.
Market demand for heavy rare earths outside China is around 400 tpy, the company said last week.
China introduced export controls on dysprosium and terbium in April 2025 following the announcement of higher tariffs on China by US President Donald Trump. China then strengthened controls on exports to Japan at the beginning of this year following comments on Taiwan by Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
China has exported no dysprosium oxide or terbium oxide directly to Japan this year, according to Chinese customs data.
Japanese magnet makers have been using their stockpiles of heavy rare earths this year, according to traders.

Manufacturers reduce heavy rare earth usage

At the same time the increase in heavy rare earth prices outside China has caused magnet producers to reduce their reliance on the elements through technological improvements.
Industry participants said consumption of dysprosium and terbium per unit of NdFeB magnet production has steadily declined over recent years, a trend they expect to continue.
Innovations including grain boundary diffusion, changes to grain size and the use of alternative alloying elements have allowed manufacturers to improve magnetic performance while reducing heavy rare earth content.
Despite this, participants stressed that dysprosium and terbium will remain critical inputs for many high-performance magnet applications in the foreseeable future, even if usage per magnet continues to decline.
“[Dysprosium] and [terbium] will be in demand, no question. But unit consumption has gone down and will continue to go down,” one market participant said.

Supply challenges remain outside China

One producer source described current market conditions as a period of “artificial constraint,” noting that prices have been driven higher by export restrictions.
While significant new magnet manufacturing capacity is planned globally, securing sufficient neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) feedstock and expanding separation capacity outside China remain major challenges, some sources said.

Spiky AI Loads Are Forcing a Rethink of Data Center Power

Aaron Larson Aaron Larson

SHARE:
Spiky AI Loads Are Forcing a Rethink of Data Center Power
The sheer scale of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers dominates the conversation about their power needs. But the way these facilities draw electricity may be the harder problem for utilities and on-site generators to solve. That is the view of Brad Witter, senior vice president of Industrial Digital at Generac, who discussed the issue on The POWER Podcast .
Witter said the industry’s answer is increasingly energy storage: batteries and fast-acting inverters that sit between the load and the grid, smoothing demand and riding through faults. Proving that those systems will work together at utility scale, he added, will depend as much on simulation as on hardware.

Three Problems, Not One

Witter described the challenge in three parts: magnitude, spikiness, and fault intolerance. On magnitude, he pointed to a data center proposed in Utah that he said equals the entire state’s load.
Size alone does not capture the risk, however. AI training clusters, in which thousands of GPUs (graphics processing units) work on a single model, change state together, Witter said.

...

Utilities Set the Terms

Developers want to go faster and utilities want to go slower, Witter said, because a utility cannot add that much capacity to an already strained system on short notice. The practical result, he said, is that many utilities are asking large loads for two things. The first is to bring their own generation, such as turbines or fuel cells, to bridge the gap while the utility catches up. The second is to behave differently once connected, limiting both the spikiness of their demand and their response to grid faults.
Asked whether utilities are in the driver’s seat, Witter said, “I would cautiously say yes,” noting that community benefits and revenue also give utilities reasons to move quickly. He said he expects hyperscalers to take on a larger share of the required investment in future interconnection agreements, and that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) is getting involved. He described hyperscalers’ willingness to build their own natural gas power plants as a bridge as unprecedented, and characterized the current market as “a land grab.”

Batteries as the Buffer

The scale of conventional backup alone is substantial, Witter said. A 200-MW site, he noted, could require hundreds of generators. To meet utility requirements and still protect on-site equipment, he said, facilities need a buffer in the form of energy storage, which flattens load swings and provides ride-through support during faults. He described storage as almost a necessity for some utility requirements, “table stakes” for securing an interconnection agreement.
Witter expects that buffer to come from two directions.

...

Proving It Before Building It

Validating these architectures is its own challenge. “You can’t do a proof of concept with a half a gigawatt of infrastructure,” Witter said, and no one will fund a multibillion-dollar test case. Manufacturers must show that equipment meets specifications on paper, he said, but how the pieces interact is “way more important” than whether each one complies individually. Utility-scale simulation, he said, is the only way to build confidence before committing at full scale.
Witter said labs such as the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR, formerly the National Renewable Energy Laboratory [NREL]) are partnering with manufacturers on hybrid testing that mixes real hardware with simulation, and that Generac has an ongoing effort with the lab. He added that utilities now commonly require modeling evidence in interconnection submissions, showing how a facility’s systems would respond to specified grid disturbances.
That integration challenge also shapes Generac’s strategy, according to Witter. He said the company has added switchgear, packaging, and transfer switch capabilities and is investing heavily in battery storage, because customers increasingly want a single partner and the orchestration involved is far more complex than the “couple wires” that traditionally tie backup power together. He said Generac’s architecture remains open to third-party equipment.
AI itself is part of the answer, Witter added. He said Generac uses it for predictive failure algorithms and manufacturing quality, and that large language models may speed the simulation work needed to prove these systems. He called it “an ironic circular loop,” with AI creating the problem it will help solve.

What Success Looks Like

Looking five years out, Witter said the data centers that got their power strategy right will be the ones that got online at all. Reaching an actionable agreement with the utility is among the biggest hurdles, he said, and many of the technologies involved are not yet fully proven. “The ones that get it right are the ones that work,” he said.
For developers that must build bridging power now, he said, the greatest benefit will go to those who plan how that equipment will support the site once utility power arrives, so nothing has to be ripped out and replaced.
To hear the full interview with Witter, listen to The POWER Podcast .

Grid interconnection has become one of the factors that constrain AI infrastructure scaling , depending on local competition for scarce capacity on the grid : the regional rules that order and prioritize connection requests, and the site’s behavior on the grid which determine exact design requirements.

How does the grid interconnection process work?

Data center grid interconnection is the process through which a grid operator studies a data center’s request for power and decides whether, when and on what terms the site can connect.
A study answers a plain question: can the lines and substations near the site carry the new demand, in normal operation and when something fails? When the answer is no, the study also names the upgrades needed, with any grid connection agreement conditional on these being implemented.
The interconnection process can be broken down into what is needed to get a grid connection agreement and what is needed to get from a signed agreement to an energized site. The first step decides how early a project can apply and what proof it must bring.
The point at which a project may apply is set nationally and differs by country.

Rules on who gets capacity are one half of the change. The other half concerns how a data center behaves once it is connected, and that behavior now shapes what operators ask for before they connect one.
